articles.title: Rochdale mum diagnosed with breast cancer after routine NHS screening
articles.excerpt: Sarah Hickman, 50, encourages women to attend NHS breast screenings after her cancer was detected early during a routine mammogram.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale mother, Sarah Hickman, has been diagnosed with breast cancer following a routine NHS screening, prompting her to urge other women to attend their appointments. At 50 years old, Sarah received her invitation for a mammogram and attended without any health concerns. However, just a day later, she was called back for further tests at the Breast Unit at Bolton NHS Foundation Trust.

After undergoing additional imaging, an ultrasound, and a biopsy, doctors confirmed that Sarah had a small breast cancer detected at a very early stage. Reflecting on her experience, she described it as a 'textbook case' and expressed gratitude for the NHS screening process, which allowed for early detection before any symptoms appeared.

Sarah's case highlights the importance of regular breast screenings, especially for women aged 50 and over, who are invited for routine mammograms every three years. Early detection can significantly improve treatment outcomes and survival rates, making it crucial for women to take these invitations seriously.

As Sarah continues her treatment, she hopes her story will encourage others to prioritise their health and attend NHS screenings. Women in Rochdale and beyond are reminded that these screenings can save lives, and they should not hesitate to book their appointments.

articles.title: Bridge Street in Heywood closed over building safety concerns
articles.excerpt: GMFRS says firefighters attended for around two hours and 40 minutes after concerns about a building structure. The road's reopening remains unconfirmed.
articles.content_html:
Firefighters attended concerns about a building structure near Bridge Street in Heywood for around two hours and 40 minutes on Saturday 24 October, according to an updated GMFRS statement reported by the Bury Times.

Update: 12.55pm GMT, Sunday 25 October 2026

The fire service said one engine from Heywood was called at about 6.30pm on Saturday. Crews inspected the building and made the area safe alongside Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council.

the source reported that Bridge Street was closed by emergency services. Its photographs showed a police cordon, a marked police car blocking access and a fire engine.

articles.title: Accrington Stanley thrash Rochdale 5-0 in League Two clash
articles.excerpt: Accrington Stanley secured a dominant 5-0 victory over Rochdale, marking their biggest away win in Football League history and extending their unbeaten run to nine games.
articles.content_html:
Accrington Stanley delivered a commanding performance against Rochdale, winning 5-0 in a League Two match on October 24, 2026. Tyler Walton scored twice, helping his team extend their unbeaten streak to nine games across all competitions. This victory marks Accrington's largest away win in their Football League history, a significant achievement for the team.

The match saw Accrington take control early, with Josh Woods opening the scoring in the 14th minute with a low shot from 20 yards after Rochdale goalkeeper Sam Waller misplayed the ball. Charlie Warren followed up with a goal in the 38th minute, striking from the edge of the box after a clever pass from Walton. Walton then added to the scoreline just before half-time with a well-placed shot from inside the box, leaving Rochdale trailing 3-0 at the break.

In the second half, Walton scored again in the 51st minute, converting a rebound after Waller saved a shot from Joe Anderson. Substitute Alex Henderson capped off the rout in the 66th minute, finishing a well-executed team move from close range. The result left Rochdale fans frustrated, as their team has now gone five matches without a win, leading to boos from the home crowd at the final whistle.

Accrington's manager, John Doolan, expressed pride in his team's performance and set a target for the play-offs, noting that they are now just one point off the play-off positions in League Two. This win not only boosts Accrington's confidence but also raises questions about Rochdale's current form and what changes may be needed to turn their season around.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.summary: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.body:
Short answer up front: the house, its date and fabric are documented; the murder tale and the angry spirit are part of oral and printed folklore rather than verified history.

Clegg Hall stands where the lane named for it climbs from the Roch to Smithy Bridge. Historic England lists the building as Grade II* (List Entry Number 1309615), dated to about 1610 and probably built for Theophilus Ashton; the list entry gives the grid reference SD9224214490 and a full architectural description of the porch, mullioned windows and interior features. These are matters of record you can look up on the National Heritage List for England. (Historic England's entry is the clearest, contemporary source for the building itself.)

The boggart story that brings visitors and late walkers to peer at the windows is older in print than the present stone house. Nineteenth century folklorists recorded a dramatic tradition: a grasping uncle, two orphan children disposed of so that the estate could be seized, and the afterwards-haunting of the place by a “Clegg Hall Boggart.” John Roby published a version in his Traditions of Lancashire; local writers and collectors repeated variants and an associated ballad. These accounts are the primary sources for the tale as a piece of Lancashire folk narrative.

Local historians have been explicit about the difference between the two kinds of source. The 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale (Butterworth) notes the same tradition but warns that Roby’s retelling is “pure imagination” and that, although a ghost tradition was current in living memory and even gave rise to the local proverb “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” the violent episode is not supported by contemporary legal or manorial records cited in the book. In short, the building and its succession of owners are documented; the murderous episode lives in oral tradition and Victorian collectors' pages.

What the archives do show is a traceable ownership and building history. Butterworth’s parish history and the Victoria County History note the medieval family names associated with the site, the sale of the “capital messuage of Clegg called Clegg Hall” in the early 17th century, and the present house’s likely early-17th-century date. Historic England cites those county histories in its list entry for the architectural description. Those documentary strands are evidence of place and people; they do not, however, supply a contemporaneous 13th- or 14th-century record proving the murders described in the boggart legend.

That distinction matters because Victorian and earlier collectors often shaped and embellished what they heard. Folklore collectors were not court clerks; they recorded stories people told, sometimes smoothing gaps with imaginative detail. The Clegg Hall boggart is one of several regional boggarts recorded in Lancashire folklore, a useful example of how local names and proverbs can preserve a tale even when the archival trail is thin.

So does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there an archival, contemporaneous record that the alleged murders took place and left restless spirits?” the answer is no: researchers citing the local histories and the National Heritage List find no surviving medieval court roll or inquest that corroborates the dramatic crime as a documented fact. If you mean “is the boggart alive as a story?” the answer is yes: the spirit survives in printed folklore, in local sayings and in the imagination of visitors and readers.

If you want to follow the trail yourself, two good starting points are the Historic England listing for the house (for verified architectural and legal status) and the nineteenth century sources that collected the tale, notably John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and Butterworth’s History of the Parish of Rochdale, which explicitly separates the tradition from the documentary record. Those sources show where the story comes from and where the solid evidence begins and ends; beyond that the rest belongs to local legend and its afterlife in print and conversation.

articles.title: Weather warning issued for Rochdale as Storm Boelo approaches
articles.excerpt: Residents in Rochdale are advised to prepare for potential disruption as Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain this weekend.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Rochdale are being warned to prepare for disruption as Storm Boelo approaches the borough this afternoon. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind, predicting strong gusts that could cause damage to buildings and trees, as well as affecting local rivers and roads.

Forecasters expect Storm Boelo to bring a very windy and wet spell this weekend, with strong winds spreading across northern parts of the UK on Saturday afternoon. Gusts of 55-65 mph are likely widely, with some coastal and exposed areas potentially experiencing gusts of 70-80 mph or more, particularly in Scotland and the far north of England.

The storm follows closely on the heels of Storm Austen, which recently impacted the south, south-west, and parts of Wales, with winds reaching up to 84 mph. Residents are encouraged to stay updated on weather conditions and take necessary precautions to ensure their safety during the storm's passage.

As Storm Boelo is expected to persist overnight and through much of Sunday, it is crucial for local residents to remain vigilant and prepared for possible disruptions. This weather event highlights the importance of being aware of severe weather warnings and taking proactive measures to protect homes and property.

articles.title: Regeneration scheme near Rochdale station progresses with new homes
articles.excerpt: A regeneration project around Rochdale station is advancing, with 81 homes under construction and plans for 33 new apartments, enhancing connectivity to the town centre.
articles.content_html:
A significant regeneration scheme around Rochdale station is making notable progress, with 81 homes currently under construction adjacent to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This development is part of a broader initiative aimed at improving connectivity between the train station and the town centre, which has historically been a purposeful distance apart.

In addition to the homes being built, plans are underway for 33 new apartments on a brownfield site located at the junction of Maclure Road and Station Road. This project is particularly significant as it will feature the first affordable net zero homes in the housing scheme, aligning with modern sustainability goals.

The regeneration project, which received approval several years ago, has secured £15 million in funding. Local authorities faced challenges in attracting investment for the project until last year, but the current construction is already benefiting the local economy and community. John Rennie Place, a key component of the scheme, is scheduled for completion in December 2027.

This development not only aims to enhance the residential landscape of Rochdale but also seeks to transform the area around the station, which has shifted from a focus on transporting goods to serving passengers. As the project progresses, it is expected to contribute positively to the local community and economy.

Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton, is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. articles.title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts. A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts. Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies. As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. articles.title: Rochdale housing development delayed again due to flooding concerns
articles.excerpt: The planning committee has deferred a decision on a housing scheme in Bamford, citing insufficient drainage details and historical flooding issues.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale planning committee has once again delayed a decision on a proposed housing development in Bamford, which aims to build 45 homes as part of a larger 450-home project. The committee's latest meeting on October 22 revealed ongoing concerns about drainage and flooding on the site, which is located behind Greenvale.

In August, the committee had previously deferred the application from Wain Homes, expressing the need for more detailed plans to address historic drainage issues. Councillors noted that without a comprehensive masterplan for the entire development, they could not make an informed decision. The site, which was removed from green belt status under the Greater Manchester housing strategy, has been flagged for its seasonal flooding problems.

Objector Lisa Bailey highlighted the site's history of flooding, stating that the area is 'seasonally wet ground'. She urged the committee to ensure that infrastructure and access issues are adequately addressed before any development proceeds. Coun Stephen Anstee remarked on the unusually high number of conditions attached to the application, indicating that the proposal is not yet ready for approval.

Wain Homes' planning agent, Stephen Harris, argued that a flood risk management assessment was included in their application and that the other developers involved in the wider scheme had no objections. However, the committee decided to defer the application again, requesting a full report on drainage management from Wain Homes before proceeding.

articles.title: Rochdale wins gold at Britain in Bloom awards, crowned champion
articles.excerpt: Rochdale has been awarded gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, securing the title of overall winner in the Town Centres and City Centres category.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has achieved a remarkable victory by winning gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards, being crowned the overall champion in the Town Centres and City Centres category. This accolade places Rochdale ahead of competitors such as Floral Godalming from the Southeast and Shaftesbury in Bloom from the South, as well as Sidcup Partners Limited from London.

The town's success in this prestigious competition is a continuation of its strong performance in recent years, having previously secured gold in 2018 and being named Best Small City in 2022. Last year, Middleton town centre held the title, making this win particularly significant as it keeps the award within the borough.

Judges praised Rochdale for its vibrant floral displays, which were provided by Bowlee Garden Nursery, as well as its recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness. They highlighted the pride, teamwork, and dedication of the community, along with the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships that exceeded the gold standard in horticulture and environmental responsibility.

Rochdale's historic Baillie Street Quarter and the striking murals created during the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival were also noted for showcasing the town's culture and civic pride. This recognition not only celebrates the town's beauty but also reflects the ongoing regeneration efforts supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant.
